items.followUp: Define translatory motion and give one example.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for defining motion about an axis.
rubric.description: Defines rotatory motion as rotation about an axis.
rubric.how: Look for a body rotating around an axis, usually a fixed axis.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for a valid example.
rubric.description: Gives one example of rotatory motion.
rubric.how: Accept examples such as a rotating fan or wheel.

modelAnswer: Rotatory motion is the motion of a body about a fixed axis.
Example: The blades of a rotating fan show rotatory motion.

items.followUp: Convert 72 km h⁻¹ into m s⁻¹.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for using the correct conversion factor or equivalent method.
rubric.description: Uses the conversion from km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹.
rubric.how: Look for multiplying the speed by 5/18, or converting kilometres to metres and hours to seconds.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for the correct converted speed with unit.
rubric.how: Check that the final numerical value is 10 and the unit is m s⁻¹.

modelAnswer: Given: v = 36 km h⁻¹.
Conversion: 1 km h⁻¹ = 5/18 m s⁻¹.
v = 10 m s⁻¹.

items.followUp: Why can a passenger standing in a bus fall forward when the bus stops suddenly?

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for identifying inertia or the body's tendency to maintain its state of motion.
rubric.description: Explains that the body tends to maintain its state of rest or motion due to inertia.
rubric.how: Look for inertia, or an explanation that the body continues its previous state of motion when the bus changes motion suddenly.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for connecting inertia to the danger of falling from the roof.
rubric.description: States that this can make a person lose balance and fall from the bus roof.
rubric.how: Look for a clear consequence such as losing balance or falling.

modelAnswer: Due to inertia, a person on the roof tends to maintain the previous state of motion when the bus starts, stops, or turns suddenly.
The person may lose balance and fall from the roof, so travelling there is dangerous.

items.followUp: Why does a passenger move forward when a moving bus stops suddenly?

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for identifying oil as a lubricant between moving surfaces.
rubric.description: States that oil forms a lubricating layer between moving parts.
rubric.how: Look for oil or lubricant separating the surfaces.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for explaining that the layer reduces friction.
rubric.description: Explains that oiling lowers friction between the moving parts.
rubric.how: Look for an explicit connection between lubrication and reduced friction.

modelAnswer: Oil forms a thin lubricating layer between the moving surfaces.
This reduces direct contact and friction between the parts.

items.followUp: What happens to the momentum of a gun and bullet when the gun is fired?

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for invoking conservation of momentum.
rubric.description: States that momentum is conserved when the gun is fired.
rubric.how: Look for conservation of momentum or equivalent wording that total momentum remains unchanged.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for explaining the gun's backward recoil as the bullet moves forward.
rubric.description: States that the gun recoils in the direction opposite to the bullet's motion.
rubric.how: Look for the gun moving backward or opposite to the bullet.

modelAnswer: Before firing, the gun and bullet are at rest, so their total momentum is zero.
When the bullet moves forward, the gun moves backward to conserve momentum; this backward motion is called recoil.

items.followUp: Define torque and give one example of its effect.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for defining a couple by its two forces.
rubric.description: Defines a couple as two equal, opposite, parallel forces acting along different lines.
rubric.how: Look for equal and opposite parallel forces; the forces must act at separated lines of action.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for a valid example.
rubric.description: Gives an example of a couple.
rubric.how: Accept examples such as turning a steering wheel with both hands or turning a tap.

modelAnswer: A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces acting along different lines of action on a body.
Example: Two hands turning a steering wheel apply a couple.

items.followUp: Define kinetic energy and write its formula.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for defining mechanical energy as the sum of kinetic and potential energies.
rubric.description: Defines mechanical energy as the sum of kinetic and potential energy.
rubric.how: Look for both forms of energy and their sum.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for naming the types of mechanical energy.
rubric.description: Writes the two types of mechanical energy.
rubric.how: Check that both kinetic energy and potential energy are named.

modelAnswer: Mechanical energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion or position; it is the sum of its kinetic and potential energies.
The types of mechanical energy are kinetic energy and potential energy.

items.followUp: A 2 kg object moves at 10 m s⁻¹. Find its kinetic energy.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for the correct kinetic-energy formula.
rubric.description: Writes the formula for kinetic energy.
rubric.how: Look for KE = ½mv² or its equivalent.

rubric.why: Award 1 mark for the correct calculation and unit.
rubric.how: Check the substituted values give 56.25 joules.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 500 g = 0.5 kg; v = 15 m s⁻¹.
Formula: KE = ½mv².
Substitution: KE = ½ × 0.5 kg × (15 m s⁻¹)².
